blocks.text: A Square in Seville. On the right the gate of the tobacco factory. At the back, facing the audience, is a practicable bridge from one side of the stage to the other, and reached from the stage by a winding staircase on the right to beyond the factory gate. The bridge is practicable underneath. In front, on the left, is a guard-house: above that, three steps lead to a covered passage. In a rack, close to the door, are the lances of the Dragoons, with their little red and yellow flags.

At the rising of the curtain, a file of Soldiers (Dragoons of Almanza) are grouped before the guard-house, smoking, and looking at the passers-by in the square, coming and going from all parts. The scene is full of animation.

lines: In the square
What a clamor!
Some are coming, some are going;
Strange indeed are they to see!
At the gate in this vicinity
Stops each one who likes—
Talking, smoking, and looking out
To watch the passing crowd.

blocks.text: Michaela has been visible for some moments. She wears a blue petticoat, and her hair falls over her shoulders. She perceives the Soldiers, and stands hesitating, not knowing if to advance or recede.

lines: Look an instant at that fair one.
It seems with us she fain would speak.
She dares not; but draws near, and glances.
To encourage her we ought.
Who are you seeking for, fair maid?
I’m seeking for a brigadier.
Indeed! Here am I.
You are not he. Don Jose he is called.
Is he not to you known?
Don Jose is not to us known.
Is it so? How shall I find him?
He is not brigadier in this troop.
Then he is not with you?
No, fair one; he’s not of ours.
But, amidst the many, he may be
Of the guard now coming here
To replace us in this post.
He will be of the guard now coming
To replace us in our post.
But whil’st he’s coming
It will not be disagreeable
(And to us a great pleasure)
If within the house you enter
Indeed.
It is the truth.
No, no, no, no.
You to enter need not fear.
On my honor I promise you
That from all you will receive
Best and heartiest welcomes.
Of it I’m sure; but, nevertheless
It suits me best now to return.
I will come again when the guard
In your post replaces you.
You ought to stay.
No, no, no, no. I must depart.
Good-bye to you all!
The bird has flown!
No one need fret.
What shall we do now?
Best watch who comes and goes.
In the place what a clamor, &c.

blocks.text: The Square fills again with the people, who had ceased during Michaela’s scene, and is lively as before.

A military march of fifes and trumpets is heard in the distance. The Relief Guard arrive. An officer goes from his post. The Soldiers take their lances and place themselves in a line before the guard-house. The people on the right gather in groups, looking on. The march sounds nearer. The Guard appear on the left, and cross the bridge: first, two Trumpeters and two Fifers; then a band of street Lads, imitating the step of the Dragoons. After the Lads the Officer Zuniga and the Brigadier Jose; then Dragoons, armed with lances.

lines: Follow we the guard that’s changing.
Quick at their heels! See, here we are!
Trumpets, strike up! be ready!
Ta, ra-ta-ta, ta, ta, ta, ra.
Each one put himself in order,
Like dragoons, all in a row;
Quick march; now all be steady—
One—two—in time we go,
Shoulders thrown back, chests well forward,
At them look, example take;
Left foot, right foot, strike the pavement,
Steady all, make no mistake.
Follow we the guard now changing,
At their heels, see! here we are!
Trumpets, strike up! be ready!
Ta, ra-ta-ta, ta, ta, ta, ra.

blocks.text: The Guard, just arrived, place themselves on the right in front of the Guard relieved. The Officers salute with the sword, and stand chatting in a low voice. The Sentry is changed.

lines: A pretty young girl
Come to ask if you were here,
With flowing hair and dress of blue—
It must be Michaela.

blocks.text: Trumpets sound. The relieved Guard pass before the New-Comers. The Street Boys, in a line, resume the place they occupied when they entered, behind the trumpets and fifes.

lines: And the guard relieved already
The place now leaves—away they go.
Trumpets all to sound are ready;
Ta-ta-ra, ta-ra, ta, ta.
Each one put himself in order,
Like dragoons all in a row;
Quick march! now all be steady;
One—two—in time we go.
Shoulders thrown back, chests well forward,
At them look—example take:
Left foot, right foot, strike the pavement,
Steady all, make no mistake.
Follow we the guard now changing,
At their heels, see! here we are!
Trumpets, strike up! be ready!
Ta-ta-ra, ta-ta, ta-ta-ra.

blocks.text: Soldiers, Lads and Spectators go off at the back; Chorus, Fifers and Trumpeters by degrees disperse. The Officer of the Guard, just arrived, during this time silently musters his Soldiers. When the Chorus is no longer heard, the Officer commands “Present!” “Carry!” “Break the line!” The Dragoons go and place their lances in the rack, and then enter the guard-house. Don Jose and the Officer remain.

lines: ’Tis in that large house the girls
Go to make cigarettes?
Yes, there, my captain; and you can assure yourself
There are some lively ones amongst them.
You know, at least, if they are handsome?
In truth, I know nothing about them,
And care very little for such toys.
I will tell you, my friend,
Who you are looking for,—
A young, fair girl;
She is named Michaela—
Golden hair and a blue petticoat.
What do you reply to this?
I answer that it is true,
I answer that I love her,
If the girls out there
Such beauty have or no.
Here they come; you can judge.

blocks.text: The factory bell is heard ringing.
Don Jose, Soldiers, Young Men and Cigar Girls.
The Square fills with Young Men coming to wait the passing of the Cigar Girls. The Soldiers enter from the guard-house. Don Jose, seated, careless of the passing scene, works at a little chain.

lines: The bell now rings. We’re here to see
The pretty faces pass along,
And follow each dark-eyed brunette
With proffered friendship and with love.

blocks.text: The Cigar Girls at this moment arrive, smoking cigarettes. They pass under the bridge, and leisurely descend the stage.

lines: What think you? Boldly they go:
True coquettes! they will not cease
Their cigarettes to smoke.
Raise we our eyes to the skies
And lightly smoke.
As upwards in perfumed clouds it flies,
On we smoke—
Pleasant smoke,
Fragrant smoke,
Cheering smoke,
It mounts so gently, lightly,
To the brain.
Soothes the soul that’s weary
To bliss from pain.
Turn we our eyes from the skies,—
All is smoke.
Words of love, how oft they prove
Nought but smoke.
Warmest sighs, fondest ties,
All end in—smoke.
But Carmencita is not here amongst you.
Here she is.
Here is Carmencita.

blocks.text: Carmen appears, in the attitude and dress described in Mérimée’s novel. She has an acacia flower at her mouth and a bouquet in her bodice. All the Young Men surround and speak to her. She coquets with all. Jose raises his eyes and looks at Carmen, and quietly goes on with his work.

lines: Carmen, all here wait for you alone.
Carmen, now be kind; turn this way awhile,
When will you love?—we fain would know.
When shall I be in love? Truly I don’t know.
Perhaps never—and, perhaps to-morrow;
But for to-day—No; vain is the thought.

blocks.text: After looking at all of them.

lines: Ah! love, thou art a wilful wild bird,
And none may hope thy wings to tame,
If it please thee to be a rebel,
Say, who can try and thee reclaim?
Threats and prayers alike unheeding;
Oft ardent homage thou’lt refuse,
Whilst he who doth coldly slight thee,
Thou for thy master oft thou’lt choose.
Ah, love!
For love he is the lord of all,
And ne’er law’s icy fetters will he wear,
If thou me lovest not, I love thee,
And if I love thee, now beware!
If thou me lovest not, beware!
The bird, so fast held in thy hand,
And which thou deemedst so secure,
Mounts, in a moment, to the skies;
Nor, till he choose, can you him lure.
He comes, he goes;
At all laughs he.
Would you seize him? he gets free!
Care not for him—then he’ll prove
Thy slave instead of master—Love!
Carmen, we wait here only for thee.
Carmen, be kind; we are to thee devoted.

blocks.text: Moment of silence. The Young Men surround Carmen; she looks at them one by one, then leaves the circle and goes straight to Jose, who is at work, and flings her bouquet of flowers at him; he starts up abruptly. General burst of laughter. The bell of the factory rings a second time. The Cigar Girls and Young Men go, during the burthen of Carmen’s song. She runs off to the factory. Don Jose remains alone on the scene.

lines: What glances! what a saucy air!
To my heart direct the flowers came,
As if a plummet struck me.

blocks.text: After taking up the flowers, smells them.

lines: Subtle is the odor, and the flowers charming.
And the fair one, if witches yet there be,
One of them surely in her I behold.
Jose!
Michaela!
Here am I.
What a pleasure!
Your mother sent me hither.
Ah! tell me of her—my mother far away.
Faithful messenger from her to thee,
I bring a letter.
A letter.
And some money also;
Because a dragoon has not too much,
And, besides that—
Something else?
Indeed, I know not how—
It is something more,
And beyond gold
By a good son more prized would be.
Tell me what this may be:
Come, reveal it to me.
Yes, I will tell you.
What she has given, I will to thee render.
Your mother with me from the chapel came,
And then, lovingly, she kissed me.
“My daughter,” said she, “to the city thou dost go;
Not long the journey.
When arrived in Seville
Thou wilt seek out Jose, my beloved son;
Tell him—Thou knowest that thy mother,
By night, by day, thinks of her Jose:
For him she always prays and hopes,
And pardons him, and loves him ever
Tell all this, dearest,
In my name, to Jose.
And then this kiss, kind one,
Thou wilt to him give for me.”
A kiss from my mother?
To her son.
Jose, I give it to thee—as I promised.

blocks.text: Michaela stands on tip-toe and kisses Jose—a true mother’s kiss. Jose, moved, permits her, with his eyes on her face. Moment of silence.

lines: My home in yonder valley,
My mother lov’d shall I e’er see?
Ah, fondly in my heart I cherish
Mem’ries so dear yet to me.
Thy home in yonder valley,
Thy mother lov’d thou yet will see,
And mem’ries dear to thee.
Thou yet wilt bless the name,
Thou yet wilt fond hope cherish!
’Twill strength and courage give thee.
That one sweet hope,
That yet again thou wilt thy home
And thy dear mother once more see.
If perchance I may become the prey of evil power!
In thy abode afar thou’lt save me, mother.
And in thy kiss I yet may see
A guardian angel ever my steps guiding.
What demon? what speakest thou? I understand not.
Explain to me thy thoughts.
No, no.
Let us speak about thyself, my messenger;
Say, thou must return to the valley?
Yes, this evening; and to-morrow I shall be there.
Well, thou wilt tell her that Jose
Loves her always, blesses her;—
That he has altered; for he wishes
His mother, far away, may of her son be glad.
Thou wilt tell her this, dear one,
In my name, for Jose;
And then this kiss, oh, kindest one,
To her give thou from me.
Yes, I promise thee—in her son Jose’s name—
To her I’ll give it.
My mother, &c.
His mother, &c.
Rest thou here, my dear one,
Whilst I read this.
No, no; thou canst read it alone;
I will return later.
Why wilt thou go?
For prudence sake;
Because it looks not well to stay.
I go, but I shall come back here.
Thou wilt return?
Return I will.

blocks.text: Jose, then the Cigar Girls and an Officer.

lines: Fear not, oh, mother; thy Jose
Will obey thee; do as thou desirest.
I love Michaela; she shall be my wife.
And thy flowers, hateful witch——

blocks.text: At the instant he is about to take the flowers from his vest, a great noise is heard in the factory. The Officer comes on the stage, followed by the Soldiers.

lines: What means this uproar?

blocks.text: The Cigar Girls run out quickly and in confusion.

lines: Run, soldiers, by this way!
Run! Will no one come?
’Twas Carmencita.
No, it was not.
It was.
No, it is not true.
But yes—
But no—
’Twas she began the quarrel.
No, no; ’tis a falsehood.
Listen, gentlemen—yes, stay and listen.
La Manuelita said,
And to every one kept telling,
That she wished to buy
What think you?—a fine donkey!
And then La Carmencita,
Who at making games too bold,
Said, “A donkey, at what cost?—
You’d better buy a wolf!”
Manuelita, wild with anger,
Made an answer rude enough:
“For your promenades
No doubt a mule would suit!”
“And then able will you be
To hold your head still higher,
With two servants in the mode,
With whips, to clear the way.”
And then, without delay,
They both began to fight.
Deuce take them both!
Jose, take two dragoons with you,
And look after these simpletons.

blocks.text: Don Jose takes two Soldiers with him, and they enter the factory; during this time the Girls argue amongst themselves.

lines: ’Tis La Carmencita.
No, no; ’twas she, signor.
Oh! oh! Be off! Get away—all of you!

blocks.text: Carmen appears at the factory door, led by Don Jose, and followed by the two Dragoons.

lines: Captain, there has been a fray.
From words they came to blows,
A girl is wounded.
And by whom?
Dost thou hear? Thou canst not deny it.
Tra la la, tra la la.
You may cut, you may burn,
No answer I’ll make;
Steel and fire I defy!
Nor angel nor demon can compel me!
We’re tired of your singing.
Will you answer or not? Reply!—come!
The secret I’ll keep, and nothing I’ll tell.
If he I adore before me now stood,
I’d nought say.
If you will not tell the truth
You will sing—in prison.
In prison?—in prison?
By Bacchus! she is not accustomed
To restrain her wilfulness.

blocks.text: Speaks aside to a Soldier, who goes in search of a rope. Carmen still keeps singing in a most impertinent fashion.

lines: Pity indeed she’s so headstrong:
Very pretty to me she seems.
Charming face,—hot brained!
Come—tie her hands.

blocks.text: The Soldiers fasten her hands behind her back. All go excepting Jose and Carmen.
Carmen and Don Jose. Silence. Carmen raises her eyes and watches Jose. He goes to the back, then returns. Carmen looks at him.

lines: And where am I to go?
To prison; and I am forced to take you.
Really? Thou wilt obey the orders?
Yes; it is my duty.
Well; I tell you that in spite of duty
You will do what I say,
Because I know that you love me.
I?—love you?
Yes, my Jose.
The flowers I gave you a while since—
Know—those flowers were enchanted.
Throw them away—’tis no avail:
They have already done their work.
Speak no more! Dost thou hear me?
You must obey. Be silent!

blocks.text: Carmen looks at Jose, who draws back.

lines: Near by the ramparts of Seville
There I shall find Lillas Pastia,
We’ll dance in the gay seguidille,
And the wine-cup we’ll share.
There shall I go to find Lillas Pastia.
Yes, but ’tis folly to go alone;
Where there’s not two no love can be,
So, to keep me from being dull,
A handsome lad will come to me.
A handsome lad—deuce take it all!—
Three days ago I sent him off.
But this new love, he loves me well;
And him to choose my mind is bent.
More lovers have I than I can count;
None of them can me in bonds retain.
Free am I yet; I know not love.
Who loves me well I’ll love again;
Who wants my heart, my heart must buy.
Why linger still? the hour is nigh,
There’s no time now for delay.
With the new love I’m off,—good-bye!
There, near the ramparts of Seville,
Lillas Pastia I shall find.
There shall I dance the seguidille,
And a goblet of wine I’ll fill!
Wilt thou not be silent?
Must I tell thee yet again?
Do you think I am talking to you?
No, I’m singing to myself.
Perhaps you think you can prevent me thinking?
I am thinking of such a—handsome officer!
And who, if I liked, I could make very happy.
Carmen!
This officer is not captain yet—
Less than lieutenant—only brigadier;
Over me has he a spell cast,
And he to please me has found the way.
Carmen, I am bewitched;
But if I yield ever, and thou lovest me,
Thy promise, ah! do not forget!
Carmen, if I love thee, wilt thou love me too?
Near the ramparts of Seville
I shall Lillas Pastia find.
There shall I dance the seguidille,
And a goblet of wine I’ll fill.

blocks.text: Carmen goes and reseats herself on the stool, with her hands behind her back. The Officer enters.

lines: Here is the order. Go, then! Haste! The hour is late.
In going there I will push thee
As hard as I am able:
Fall thou on the ground—leave the rest to me.

blocks.text: Places herself between the two Dragoons; Jose is at her side. The Girls and Young Men come on the scene, kept back by the Soldiers. Carmen crosses from left to right, going toward the bridge.

lines: Love is still the lord of all;
For him no laws can fetters bear.
If thou me lovest not, I love thee;
And, if I love thee, now beware!

blocks.text: Arriving at the foot of the bridge on the right, Carmen pushes Jose, who falls to the ground. Confusion. Carmen escapes. She stops a moment in the centre of the bridge, throws the cord over the parapet, and disappears; while on the stage the Cigar Girls, with great bursts of laughter, surround the Officer.
